newsitem.title: USA: FOMC -- What is the Fed looking at?.
newsitem.headline: FOMC -- What is the Fed looking at?.

text.p: The policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee is meeting on Tuesday as uncertainty about the U.S. interest rate outlook prevails on Wall Street.

The Federal Reserve is faced with an economic equation worth the envy of the industrial world: a combination of strong growth, full employment and low, steady inflation. As an added bonus, the federal budget deficit may be wiped out in just five years.
The main question is to what extent the Fed wants its policy, credited for the lasting expansion, to be preemptive.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan and other central bankers have reiterated that achieving low inflation is the means -- and the only means -- by which the Fed can contribute to the much-desired end of solid growth and healthy job creation.
Since introducing his preemptive policy in 1994, Greenspan has repeatedly detailed how the Fed's strategy intends to prevent -- rather than fight -- inflation.
** GREENSPAN'S RECENT COMMENTS
-- "To be sure, 1997 is not 1994," Greenspan stressed in the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress in February and again, on May 8, in a speech in New York City.
In his latest speech, Greenspan made clear "our actions to tighten money market conditions in 1994, and again in March of this year" both belong to the same preemptive approach.
The difference, Greenspan stressed, is that, in 1994, the Fed "was forced to tighten monetary conditions very substantially" when the inflation-adjusted, real federal funds rate was at about zero.

Though many analysts describe the real funds rate as currently slightly restrictive, Greenspan cautioned "Yet, we must be wary," since resources, mainly in labor markets, are under pressure due to rapid growth and high consumer demand.
"Should the expected slowing in the growth of demand fail to materialize, we would need to address any emerging pressures in product and credit markets," Greenspan also said.

Many market watchers interpret the sentence as a signal the Fed does not want to raise interest rates on Tuesday, and not until prices begin to rise and market rates back up amid inflation fears -- which would make the next Fed tightening more politically acceptable.
A source close to the Fed told Reuters Greenspan's latest comments were aimed at explaining the Fed's preemptive policy in general and were not dealing with the May 20 FOMC meeting.

The source noted that Greenspan and other Fed officials repeatedly made the point that responding to emerging price pressures and rising market rates would call for higher interest rate hikes that come at a greater cost to the economy.
** THE MARKET'S VIEW:

-- In a Reuters survey of the 39 U.S. primary dealers, 21 expect no change in the 5.50-percent fed funds rate or the 5.0-percent discount rate, while 18 expect a 25-basis-point hike in the funds rate. Only three also see a 25- or 50-point hike in the discount rate.

Nomura Securities International chief economist David Resler expected a 25-point hike in the funds rate on Tuesday as the second installment in a 50-point "form of insurance" -- to cite Greenspan -- that the Fed started to take on March 25.

CS First Boston chief market strategist Matthew Alexy did not expect a rate move on Tuesday, drawing a parallel between current policy and the limited July 1995-January 1996 easing cycle -- a "process of rebalancing interest rates."
Though the two analysts differ on the timing of the next Fed move, they agreed the current cycle will not be aggressive due to the low level of inflation.
** ECONOMIC DATA :

-- Though trend growth may be higher, at least on a temporary basis, than the 2.0- to 2.5-percent range often cited by Fed officials, the 3.8-percent Gross Domestic Product growth recorded in the fourth quarter of 1996 and the 5.6-percent of the first quarter point to an overheating of the economy.

-- Most FOMC members subscribe to the belief that inflation pressures result when unemployment drops below the so-called non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU). Many have revised their view of the NAIRU to probably around 5.50 percent rather than 5.75 percent. But Fed sources said that rate cannot have dropped to April's 4.9 percent.
-- Gauges of consumer demand, such as the spring retail sales, showed a slowdown in demand. However, consumer confidence at record levels indicate a likely rebound.
